analysis.one_liner: Protects 1.5 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, blocking oil drilling.
analysis.headline: The wilderness bill for the Arctic Refuge's coastal plain drew 36 Senate cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have designated about 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain in Alaska as wilderness under the Wilderness Act. Wilderness is the strongest protection federal land can get: it permanently bars roads, motorized development, and oil and gas drilling. The bill went to the Senate environment committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a stake in the nation's public lands and wildlife: the bill would have permanently protected the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and other Arctic wildlife from industrial development, preserved a wild area in its natural state for future generations, and kept the coastal plain off the table for drilling.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a roughly 1,559,538-acre portion of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to the National Wilderness Preservation System under the Wilderness Act.
Wilderness designation is the highest level of federal land protection, permanently prohibiting oil and gas development, roads, and permanent facilities in the designated area.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which has long sought access to the Arctic Refuge coastal plain, would lose any chance to explore and drill there. Alaska's state government would forgo potential royalties and jobs tied to development on the refuge.

drawbacks.text: Wilderness protection would permanently close the coastal plain — the only part of the refuge thought to hold significant oil — to energy development, forgoing potential federal revenue, Alaska jobs, and domestic production.

The designation is irreversible in practice: once land is designated wilderness, development is barred unless Congress acts again, so opponents argue Congress should not lock away resources permanently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is straightforward and genuine: permanent protection of a unique Arctic ecosystem versus forgoing energy development and the revenue and jobs it could bring to Alaska. The bill's advocates saw the refuge's wilderness and wildlife values as outweighing that; opponents — chiefly Alaska's political establishment and the oil industry — did not. Either way, the bill never advanced far enough for the debate to actually happen.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the bill on December 2, 2015, joined by 35 Democratic senators and one independent as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the coastal plain was left without wilderness protection, keeping it available for future oil and gas development — an outcome the oil industry and Alaska's pro-drilling establishment had sought. Supporters of protection got nothing for their effort.

for.name: Michael F. Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill designating the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness and recruited 36 cosponsors.

against.name: James M. Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's independent, and no Republican signed on; the bill went nowhere in a Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently bar drilling on the coastal plain, an area the industry has long sought for exploration. Its interest in opening the refuge runs against preserving the land for the public.

Alaska's government and development interests count on royalties and jobs from opening federal lands; wilderness designation forecloses that on the refuge. Some Alaskans, including subsistence communities, instead supported protection.
